analysis.one_liner: Lowers Medicare drug costs, caps monthly insulin copays, and speeds up generic competition.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2019 with 147 Republican cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would lower what Medicare and Medicaid patients pay for prescription drugs. It redesigns the Medicare Part D benefit to shrink seniors' out-of-pocket costs, caps monthly insulin costs, forces drug makers to apply discounts at the pharmacy counter, makes manufacturers refund Medicare for portions of single-dose drugs that get thrown away, and requires companies to publicly explain large price increases. It also speeds up generic and biosimilar competition and targets middlemen practices like spread pricing in Medicaid.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would pay less out of pocket for prescription drugs, including a monthly cap on insulin costs and discounted prices applied at the pharmacy counter. Medicaid beneficiaries and taxpayers would benefit from rebate fixes and an end to abusive spread pricing. Patients waiting for cheaper alternatives would gain from faster generic and biosimilar competition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare and Medicaid patients

how_it_helps.text: Redesigns the Medicare Part D benefit so beneficiaries pay 15% instead of 25% in an initial phase, ends the coverage-gap structure, and requires manufacturers to provide discounted prices at the point of sale.
Establishes a monthly cap on what beneficiaries pay for insulin products and supplies under Medicare drug plans.

Requires manufacturers of certain expensive drugs to report and publicly explain price increases of 10% in a year or 25% over three years, with civil penalties of up to $75,000 per day for failing to report.
Makes manufacturers refund Medicare for the discarded portion of single-dose container drugs, with the money returned to the Medicare trust fund.
Includes the CREATES Act and pay-for-delay antitrust provisions to make it easier for generics and biosimilars to reach the market, and bans abusive spread pricing by middlemen in Medicaid.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would pay refunds for discarded drugs and point-of-sale discounts and would face capped Medicare add-on payments and mandatory price-increase reporting. Pharmacy benefit managers would face new transparency requirements and an end to spread pricing. Medicare drug plans would take on a different share of drug costs under the redesigned benefit.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not let Medicare negotiate drug prices or cap list prices directly; manufacturers must explain large price increases but are not prevented from making them.

Several provisions are studies and reports rather than binding action, including a Federal Trade Commission study of pharmacy benefit managers and a GAO report on pharmacy boards' conflicts of interest.
The Part D redesign restructures who pays for high-cost drugs after beneficiaries hit the out-of-pocket cap, moving costs among plans, manufacturers, and reinsurance rather than eliminating them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real, targeted relief—cheaper insulin, smaller out-of-pocket costs for seniors, refunds for wasted drugs, and faster generic competition—but it is incremental. It relies on transparency and competition rather than directly limiting what manufacturers can charge, and several provisions are studies rather than binding rules. An honest supporter would acknowledge it stops well short of the government-negotiation approaches Democrats proposed the same Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and two subcommittees, but no committee ever approved it and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Walden introduced the bill on December 9, 2019, with 147 Republican cosponsors.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees, and then to the Health and Antitrust subcommittees.
No further action—no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote—is recorded for the bill through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

The bill would have limited Medicare payment for drugs, reduced Part D cost-sharing, revised the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program, eased approval of generics and biosimilars, and required price-increase reporting by manufacturers.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, brand-name drug makers and pharmacy benefit managers kept the existing pricing system untouched, and Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries received none of the cost relief this bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and PBMs kept the status quo

for.name: Greg Walden
for.role: Ranking Member, House Energy and Commerce Committee; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 147 Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair Frank Pallone)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 9, 2019 but never scheduled a markup or committee vote; the record shows only a subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Richard Neal)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but took no recorded action on the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jerrold Nadler)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent it to its Antitrust subcommittee; took no further recorded action.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: The Democratic majority advanced its own drug pricing bill (H.R. 3) instead of this one, and this bill was never brought to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded. The sponsor and all 147 cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic majority pursued its own, more aggressive drug pricing bill instead.

industries.note: They would pay refunds for discarded drugs, point-of-sale discounts under Part D, capped Medicare add-on payments, and mandatory public reporting on large price increases—but the bill avoids government price negotiation and includes industry-backed regulatory items like over-the-counter monograph reform and orphan drug clarifications.

The bill directs an FTC study of anticompetitive PBM conduct, requires public disclosure of rebate pass-through data, and bans abusive spread pricing in Medicaid—practices that let middlemen profit from the gap between what plans pay and what pharmacies receive.
The CREATES Act, REMS access provisions, and pay-for-delay antitrust penalties would make it easier to bring lower-cost competitors to market.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D drug plans and insurers
industries.note: The benefit redesign changes how much plans pay across coverage phases and requires real-time cost-sharing tools for prescribers, shifting their cost exposure rather than simply raising or lowering it.
The spread-pricing ban and the prohibition on steering patients to PBM-owned pharmacies would ease financial pressure that middlemen practices have placed on local pharmacies.
